body_markdown: F1 buffs, and Ayrton Senna fans in particular, know the history well. The year before he heads to F1, an ascendant Senna charges through the first half of the 1983 British Formula 3 championship, winning the first nine races, only to have a devil of a time closing the deal against the comparatively unassuming Martin Brundle. It came down to the last race. A good retelling, though, never gets old. On a recent late-evening, keep-watching-car-videos-because-why-not binge, my algorithm served up *Senna vs Brundle – The season before Formula 1* . I immediately knew what I’d be doing for the next hour and a half. The documentary, directed by Mario Muth, had somehow escaped me when it was originally released in 2016 (it’s been available on Amazon). It’s now available for free. A little more than a week ago, the film went up on Muth’s YouTube page, which appears to have been dormant for years. The documentary sits alongside several detailed interviews from years ago, including Murray Walker, David Coulthard, and Will Buxton. Muth’s deep dive into the 1983 season doesn’t trade in drama like other recountings of Senna’s trajectory. Instead, it relies heavily on storytelling from those who lived the events. Brundle himself, along with his team owner, the gregarious Eddie Jordan; Senna’s team principal, Dick Bennets; legendary announcer Murray Walker; and racers Calvin Fish, Davy Jones, and others all advance the story in vivid detail. It’s an incredible group of people, any one of whom would have been a captivating interview on their own. Viewers used to the faster pace of today’s popular documentaries may wish that Muth pressed the accelerator a bit more to advance the story. However, the facets of the story revealed by the methodical interviews—Senna’s pressure on the Italian engine builders, how the personality of each of the team principals provided a yin to their driver’s yang, how both drivers grew from their intense battle—are well worth the time. “Everything that mushroomed through his Grand Prix career was there to be seen in 1983,” said Brundle of Senna. That includes[Senna’s feeling of destiny](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/ayrton-sennas-top-5-formula-1-drives-ranked/) ; when Brundle went on a three-race win streak starting at Silverstone in the middle of the season, the Brazilian almost didn’t know what to do. The rest of the year was marked by Senna’s inconsistency, either winning or wrecking out. Ultimately, though, the 1983 British F3 championship steeled both drivers for their rise to the ranks of F1. Senna perhaps became even more wily that year, and Brundle’s brilliant determination against the man who everyone knew was a hero-in-waiting elevated his skills and his prospects. *Senna vs Brundle* captured this stepping-stone year well, and should be on any hardcore fan’s watch list.
